thread.title: Hyperinflation fears on Wall Street: You’ve got to be kidding, right?

author: Terry Ponick
title: Hyperinflation fears on Wall Street: You’ve got to be kidding, right?
text:
Hyperinflation fears on Wall Street: You’ve got to be kidding, right? written by Terry Ponick Feb 7, 2018 
WASHINGTON, February 6, 2018: Look out for hyperinflation! You really begin to suspect the sanity, if not the intelligence, of investment analysts and economists when they start hyperventilating about catastrophic economic events that are highly unlikely to happen. Lately, they’ve been freaking out over America’s allegedly imminent confrontation with hyperinflation. Read also: Turnaround Tuesday on Wall Street? Maybe. Just flip a coin 
This coming hyperinflationary surge, so these fearmongers say, will immediately cause the American economy to tumble into a deep recession. No doubt, hyperinflation will arrive just in time to defeat the GOP in this fall’s Congressional elections. Be afraid. Be very afraid. 
Aside from predictable smart-ass analyst sniping at Apple every day – it was Goldman Sachs’ turn today – which keeps Apple’s shares (symbol: AAPL) flat-to-down, and which in turn holds back the NASDAQ and related technical indexes – the bafflegab in the investment advisory industry has become so absurd that for now, at least, investors should just turn these clowns off. 
One extended example: As 2018 begins, we’re finally getting close to the investment growth targets we should have been achieving during Barack Obama’s socialist administration as far back as 2011. That’s a milestone that would have helped Ben Bernanke achieve his higher 2 percent inflation target without printing more and more money. But no. We had to wait until after January 20, 2017, when the game changed as the economy almost immediately achieved liftoff under the new Trump administration. 
From Day 1 in the Oval Office, Trump began killing quadrillions of business-squelching and useless Federal “rules.” Even better, under Trump’s urging, the (nominally) GOP-controlled Congress finally managed to squeeze through a game-changing, highly stimulative tax cut package. After the market’s late-December bout of tax-loss selling had exhausted itself, we began 2018 with a YUGE rally that soon looked like it would never end. 
Until it did. 
All the while, even today after Monday’s brutal crash, all we’ve been hearing from most analysts is that hyperinflation, perhaps worse than Venezuela’s, is right around the corner as a result of Trump’s and the GOP’s “risky,” stimulative economic policies. 
In fact, all that’s really happening is that The average working stiff is finally getting the pay hikes he, she or it should have been getting, at least incrementally, for the past 20 years and counting; and The U.S. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is finally achieving lift-off some 6 years after it should have, again solely due to regime change in Washington. 
So why is all this bad? Beats me. That hyperinflation boogie man is beginning give off the familiar “fake news” scent. 
But what’s really going on in background indicates a great deal of fear, real or manufactured, on the part of the investing cognoscenti. Granted, interest rates have been moving up at a pretty good clip. That’s at least partially the intended effect of the Fed’s gradual tightening of core interest rates, combined with the central bank’s modest but steady unloading of all those bonds it bought over the past few years to stimulate the economy. 
The Fed’s “QE” activity involving those bond purchases was designed to put cash into a deflationary economy to offset the economy-killing effects of Obama’s do-nothing economic policies that were meant to strangle the middle class. 
That’s why at least some of the outsized increases in interest rates over the last few months have clearly been the Fed’s doing. Yet why have recent upward interest rate spikes exceeded what the Fed clearly means to accomplish? It’s actually the bond ghouls and vigilantes that are causing these big swings, not the Fed. 
It seems to me that at least some financial gurus and their media friends, including all those elite geniuses from the Harvard and Yale B-school crime dens, are trying to create a nasty recession, and soon, since their Deep State pals in Washington have not yet been able to dislodge President Trump with their increasingly absurd Russia Collusion fabulations. 
So the latest theory appears to go, inducing a nasty recession, perhaps beginning this summer, might help sour mid-term American voters on the GOP and change control of Congress, which, of course, is exactly what everyone on the left sincerely wants since no Republican can legitimately represent the American people 
What, in fact, is the problem with Trump and Congress trying to catch up on the vigorous, post-recession growth the U.S. economy should already have been enjoying for the past several years? Perhaps our betters don’t like the idea that the middle class might finally be getting the tax and wage breaks and gains they need to support their families while creating the kind of individual economic surplus that might get them to save, invest, and buy new homes like they used to. 
American business is getting better and is bound to improve further as those game-changing corporate tax cuts begin to take hold. For that reason, I think, once markets have shaken off artificial interest rate, Federal budget and hyperinflation fears, stocks should gradually resume their upward trajectory, perhaps later this month, albeit with a bit more caution and a bit less irrational exuberance, both of which are good things. 
Should these gradual shifts back to economic positivism and sanity transpire over the next few weeks, and should the Trumpian Era of Stock Market Good Feelings return, the stock market might pull a rabbit out of his hat instead of this week’s big bad bear, which may have surprised him as much as it surprised us. If that’s the case, his next random walk might be a rather sedate amble toward the positive, something that would be good for us all.
